ginglymodi: An order of ganoid fishes, including the modern gar pikes and many allied fossil forms. They have rhombic, ganoid scales, a heterocercal tail, paired fins without an axis, fulcra on the fins, and a bony skeleton, with the vertebræ convex in front and concave behind, forming a ball and socket joint. See Ganoidel.
giust: Same as Joust. Spenser. | Same as Joust. Spenser.
gimp: Smart; spruce; trim; nice. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] | A narrow ornamental fabric of silk, woolen, or cotton, often with a metallic wire, or sometimes a coarse cord, running through it; -- used as trimming for dresses, furniture, etc.
girdler: 1. One who girdles. 2. A maker of girdles. 3. (Zoöl.) An American longicorn beetle (Oncideres cingulatus) which lays its eggs in the twigs of the hickory, and then girdles each branch by gnawing a groove around it, thus killing it to provide suitable food for the larvæ.
giddiness: The quality or state of being giddy.
gipoun: A short cassock. [Written also gepoun, gypoun, jupon, juppon.] (old)
gige: The leather strap by which the shield of a knight was slung across the shoulder, or across the neck and shoulder. Meyrick (Ancient Armor).
girandole: 1. An ornamental branched candlestick. 2. A flower stand, fountain, or the like, of branching form. 3. (Pyrotechny) A kind of revolving firework. 4. (Fort.) A series of chambers in defensive mines. Farrow.
gingerly: Cautiously; timidly; fastidiously; daintily. What is't that you took up so gingerly Shak.
giddy: 1. Having in the head a sensation of whirling or reeling about; having lost the power of preserving the balance of the body, and therefore wavering and inclined to fall; lightheaded; dizzy. | To make dizzy or unsteady. (old)
given: p. p. & a. from Give, v. 1. (Math. & Logic) Granted; assumed; supposed to be known; set forth as a known quantity, relation, or premise. 2. Disposed; inclined; -- used with an adv.; as, virtuously given. Shak. 3. Stated; fixed; as, in a given time.
giggyng: The act of fastending the gige or leather strap to the shield. (old) "Gigging of shields." Chaucer.
gigue: A piece of lively dance music, in two strains which are repeated; also, the dance.
gibe: To cast reproaches and sneering expressions; to rail; to utter taunting, sarcastic words; to flout; to fleer; to scoff. Fleer and gibe, and laugh and flout. Swift. | To reproach with contemptuous words; to deride; to scoff at; to mock. Draw the beasts as I describe them, From their features, while I gibe them. Swift.
girasole: 1. (Bot.) See Heliotrope. (old) 2. (Min.) A variety of opal which is usually milk white, bluish white, or sky blue; but in a bright light it reflects a reddish color.
girth: 1. A band or strap which encircles the body; especially, one by which a saddle is fastened upon the back of a horse. 2. The measure round the body, as at the waist or belly; | To bind as with a girth. Johnson.
giddyhead: A person without thought fulness, prudence, or judgment. [Colloq.] Burton.
gibberish: Rapid and inarticulate talk; unintelligible language; unmeaning words; jargon. He, like a gypsy, oftentimes would go; All kinds of gibberish he had learnt to known. Drayton. | Unmeaning; as, gibberish language.
gigantesque: Befitting a giant; bombastic; magniloquent. The sort of mock-heroic gigantesque With which we bantered little Lilia first. Tennyson.
giblets: The inmeats, or edible viscera (heart, gizzard, liver, etc.), of poultry.
giltedged: 1. Having a gilt edge; as, gilt-edged paper. 2. Of the best quality; -- said of negotiable paper, etc. [Slang, U. S.]
giant: 1. A man of extraordinari bulk and stature. Giants of mighty bone and bold emprise. Milton. 2. A person of extraordinary strength or powers, bodily or intellectual. 3. | Like a giant; extraordinary in size, strength, or power; as, giant brothers; a giant son. Giant cell. (Anat.) See Myeloplax. -- Giant clam (Zoöl.), a bivalve shell of the genus Tridacna, esp. T.
girlish: Like, or characteristic of, a girl; of or pertaining to girlhood; innocent; artless; immature; weak; as, girlish ways; girlish grief. -- Girl"ish*ly, adv. -- Girl"ish*ness, n.
giver: One who gives; a donor; a bestower; a grantor; one who imparts or distributes. It is the giver, and not the gift, that engrosses the heart of the Christian. Kollock.
gid: A disease of sheep, characterized by vertigo; the staggers. It is caused by the presence of the CC.
gilding: 1. The art or practice of overlaying or covering with gold leaf; also, a thin coating or wash of gold, or of that which resembles gold. 2. Gold in leaf, powder, or liquid, for application to any surface. 3. Any superficial coating or appearance, as opposed to what is solid and genuine. Gilding metal, a tough kind of sheet brass from which cartridge shells are made.
gip: To take out the entrails of (herrings). | A servant. See Gyp. Sir W. Scott.
gingival: Of or pertaining to the gums. Holder.
gift: 1. Anything given; anything voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation; a present; an offering. Shall I receive by gift, what of my own, . . . I can command Milton. 2. | To endow with some power or faculty. He was gifted . . . with philosophical sagacity. I. Taylor.
girt: To gird; to encircle; to invest by means of a girdle; to measure the girth of; as, to girt a tree. We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk, And girt thee with the sword. Shak. | Bound by a cable; -- used of a vessel so moored by two anchors that she swings against one of the cables by force of the current or tide.
giltedge: 1. Having a gilt edge; as, gilt-edged paper. 2. Of the best quality; -- said of negotiable paper, etc. [Slang, U. S.]
ginglymus: A hinge joint; an articulation, admitting of flexion and extension, or motion in two directions only, as the elbow and the ankle.
giblet: Made of giblets; as, a giblet pie.
giraffe: An African ruminant (Camelopardalis giraffa) related to the deers and antelopes, but placed in a family by itself; the camelopard. It is the tallest of animals, being sometimes twenty feet from the hoofs to the top of the head. Its neck is very long, and its fore legs are much longer than its hind legs.
gibbon: Any arboreal ape of the genus Hylobates, of which many species and varieties inhabit the East Indies and Southern Asia. They are tailless and without cheek pouches, and have very long arms, adapted for climbing. Note: The white-handed gibbon (Hylobates lar), the crowned (H. pilatus), the wou-wou or singing gibbon (H. agilis), the siamang, and the hoolock.
ginseng: A plant of the genus Aralia, the root of which is highly valued as a medicine among the Chinese. The Chinese plant (Aralia Schinseng) has become so rare that the American (A. quinquefolia) has largely taken its place, and its root is now an article of export from America to China.
ginhouse: A building where cotton is ginned.
gipsire: A kind of pouch formerly worn at the girdle. Ld. Lytton. A gipser all of silk, Hung at his girdle, white as morné milk. Chaucer.
gilt: Gilded; covered with gold; of the color of gold; golden yellow. "Gilt hair" Chaucer. | 1. Gold, or that which resembles gold, laid on the surface of a thing; gilding. Shak. 2. Money. (old) "The gilt of France." Shak.
gimbals: A contrivance for permitting a body to incline freely in all directions, or for suspending anything, as a barometer, ship's compass, chronometer, etc., so that it will remain plumb, or level, when its support is tipped, as by the rolling of a ship.
ginglymoidal: Pertaining to, or resembling, a ginglymus, or hinge joint; ginglyform.
ginglymoid: Pertaining to, or resembling, a ginglymus, or hinge joint; ginglyform.
gigantomachy: A war of giants; especially, the fabulous war of the giants against heaven.
ginkgo: A large ornamental tree (Ginkgo biloba) from China and Japan, belonging to the Yew suborder of Coniferæ. Its leaves are so like those of some maidenhair ferns, that it is also called the maidenhair tree.
gipser: A kind of pouch formerly worn at the girdle. Ld. Lytton. A gipser all of silk, Hung at his girdle, white as morné milk. Chaucer.
gizzard: 1. (Anat.) The second, or true, muscular stomach of birds, in which the food is crushed and ground, after being softened in the glandular stomach (crop), or lower part of the esophagus; the gigerium. 2. (Zoöl.) (a) A thick muscular stomach found in many invertebrate animals. (b) A stomach armed with chitinous or shelly plates or teeth, as in certain insects and mollusks.
gith: The corn cockle; also anciently applied to the Nigella, or fennel flower.
giglot: A wanton; a lascivious or light, giddy girl. (old) The giglet is willful, and is running upon her fate. Sir W. Scott. | Giddi; light; inconstant; wanton. (old) "O giglot fortune!" Shak.
gigot: 1. A leg of mutton. 2. A small piece of flesh; a slice. (old) The rest in giggots cut, they spit. Chapman.
gild: 1. To overlay with a thin covering of gold; to cover with a golden color; to cause to look like gold. "Gilded chariots." Pope. No more the rising sun shall gild the morn. Pope. 2. To make attractive; to adorn; to brighten. Let oft good humor, mild and gay, Gild the calm evening of your day. Trumbull. 3. To give a fair but deceptive outward appearance to; to embellish;
ging: Same as Gang, n., 2. (old) There is a knot, a ging, a pack, a conspiracy against me. Shak.
gipsymoth: A tussock moth (Ocneria dispar) native of the Old World, but accidentally introduced into eastern Massachusetts about 1869, where its caterpillars have done great damage to fruit, shade, and forest trees of many kinds. The male gypsy moth is yellowish brown, the female white, and larger than the male. In both sexes the wings are marked by dark lines and a dark lunule.
giftedness: The state of being gifted. Echard.
ginging: The lining of a mine shaft with stones or bricks to prevent caving.
gibaro: The offspring of a Spaniard and an Indian; a Spanish-Indian mestizo. [Sp. Amer.]
gimmer: A piece of mechanism; mechanical device or contrivance; a gimcrack. (old) Bp. Hall. Shak.
gimcrack: A trivial mechanism; a device; a toy; a pretty thing. Arbuthnot.
girl: 1. A young person of either sex; a child. (old) Chaucer. 2. A female child, from birth to the age of puberty; a young maiden. 3. A female servant; a maidservant. [U. S.] 4. (Zoöl.) A roebuck two years old. [Prov. Eng.]
gibfish: The male of the salmon. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.
girdlestead: 1. That part of the body where the girdle is worn. (old) Sheathed, beneath his girdlestead. Chapman. 2. The lap. There fell a flower into her girdlestead. Swinburne.
gimbal: A contrivance for permitting a body to incline freely in all directions, or for suspending anything, as a barometer, ship's compass, chronometer, etc., so that it will remain plumb, or level, when its support is tipped, as by the rolling of a ship.
gill: 1. (Anat.) An organ for aquatic respiration; a branchia. Fishes perform respiration under water by the gills. Ray. Note: Gills are usually lamellar or filamentous appendages, through which the blood… | A two-wheeled frame for transporting timber. [Prov. Eng.]
gismondine: A native hydrated silicate of alumina, lime, and potash, first noticed near Rome.
gieseckite: A mineral occurring in greenish gray six-sided prisms, having a greasy luster. It is probably a pseudomorph after elæolite.
gilly: A boy or young man; a manservant; a male attendant, in the Scottish Highlands. Sir W. Scott.
give: 1. To bestow without receiving a return; to confer without compensation; to impart, as a possession; to grant, as authority or permission; to yield up or allow. For generous lords had rather give… | 1. To give a gift or gifts. 2. To yield to force or pressure; to relax; to become less rigid; as, the earth gives under the feet. 3. To become soft or moist. (old) Bacon . 4. To move; to recede.
girdle: A griddle. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] | 1. That which girds, encircles, or incloses; a circumference; a belt; esp., a belt, sash, or article of dress encircling the body usually at the waist; a cestus. Within the girdle of these walls.
gigantean: Like a giant; mighty; gigantic. (old) Dr. H. More.
gibstaff: 1. A staff to guage water, or to push a boat. 2. A staff formerly used in fighting beasts on the stage. (old) Bailey.
gillhouse: A shop where gill is sold. Thee shall each alehouse, thee each gillhouse mourn. Pope.
gillian: A girl; esp., a wanton; a gill. (old) Beau. & Fl.
giallolino: A term variously employed by early writers on art, though commonly designating the yellow oxide of lead, or massicot. Fairholt.
gibbous: 1. Swelling by a regular curve or surface; protuberant; convex; as, the moon is gibbous between the half-moon and the full moon. The bones will rise, and make a gibbous member. Wiseman. 2. Hunched; hump-backed. (old) Sir T. Browne. -- Gib"bous*ly, adv. -- Gib"bous*ness, n.
gilamonster: A large tuberculated lizard (Heloderma suspectum) native of the dry plains of Arizona, New Mexico, etc. It is the only lizard known to have venomous teeth.
gittith: A musical instrument, of unknown character, supposed by some to have been used by the people of Gath, and thence obtained by David. It is mentioned in the title of Psalms viii., lxxxi., and lxxxiv. Dr. W. Smith.
gilthead: A marine fish. The name is applied to two species: (a) The Pagrus, or Chrysophrys, auratus, a valuable food fish common in the Mediterranean (so named from its golden-colored head); -- called also giltpoll. (b) The Crenilabrus melops, of the British coasts; -- called also golden maid, conner, sea partridge.
giggle: To laugh with short catches of the breath or voice; to laugh in a light, affected, or silly manner; to titter with childish levity. Giggling and laughing with all their might At the piteous hap of… | A kind of laugh, with short catches of the voice or breath; a light, silly laugh.
gibel: A kind of carp (Cyprinus gibelio); -- called also Prussian carp.
gibraltar: 1. A strongly fortified town on the south coast of Spain, held by the British since 1704; hence, an impregnable stronghold. 2. A kind of candy sweetmeat, or a piece of it; -- called, in full, Gibraltar rock.
gillflirt: A thoughtless, giddy girl; a flirt-gill. Sir W. Scott.
gigerium: The muscular stomach, or gizzard, of birds.
gibbostity: The state of being gibbous or gibbose; gibbousness.
gigantic: 1. Of extraordinary size; like a giant. 2. Such as a giant might use, make, or cause; immense; tremendous; extraordinarly; as, gigantic deeds; gigantic wickedness. Milton. When descends on the Atlantic The gigantic Strom wind of the equinox. Longfellow.
ginnycarriage: A small, strong carriage for conveying materials on a railroad. [Eng.]
girtline: A gantline. Hammock girtline, a line rigged for hanging out hammocks to dry.
gigantology: An account or description of giants.
gibbartas: One of several finback whales of the North Atlantic; -- called also Jupiter whale. [Written also jubartas, gubertas, dubertus.]
gisarm: A weapon with a scythe-shaped blade, and a separate long sharp point, mounted on a long staff and carried by foot soldiers.
giganticide: The act of killing, or one who kills, a giant. Hallam.
gismondite: A native hydrated silicate of alumina, lime, and potash, first noticed near Rome.
gingerbread: A kind of plain sweet cake seasoned with ginger, and sometimes made in fanciful shapes. "Gingerbread that was full fine." Chaucer. Gingerbread tree (Bot.), the doom palm; -- so called from the resemblance of its fruit to gingerbread. See Doom Palm. -- Gingerbread work, ornamentation, in architecture or decoration, of a fantastic, trivial, or tawdry character.
girondist: A member of the moderate republican party formed in the French legislative assembly in 1791. The Girondists were so called because their leaders were deputies from the department of La Gironde. | Of or pertaining to the Girondists. [Written also Girondin.]
ginshop: A shop or barroom where gin is sold as a beverage. [Colloq.]
giantship: The state, personality, or character, of a giant; -- a compellation for a giant. His giantship is gone somewhat crestfallen. Milton.
gibber: To speak rapidly and inarticulately. Shak.
gimmor: A piece of mechanism; mechanical device or contrivance; a gimcrack. (old) Bp. Hall. Shak.
giber: One who utters gibes. B. Jonson.
gillyflower: 1. A name given by old writers to the clove pink (Dianthus Caryophyllus) but now to the common stock (Matthiola incana), a cruciferous plant with showy and fragrant blossoms, usually purplish, but often pink or white. 2. A kind of apple, of a roundish conical shape, purplish red color, and having a large core. [Written also gilliflower.] Clove gillflower, the clove pink.
giaour: An infidel; -- a term applied by Turks to disbelievers in the Mohammedan religion, especially Christrians. Byron.
gingham: A kind of cotton or linen cloth, usually in stripes or checks, the yarn of which is dyed before it is woven; -- distinguished from printed cotton or prints.
girlhood: State or time of being a girl.
gib: To act like a cat. (old) Beau. & Fl. | A piece or slip of metal or wood, notched or otherwise, in a machine or structure, to hold other parts in place or bind them together, or to afford a bearing surface;
gist: 1. A resting place. (old) These quails have their set gists; to wit, ordinary resting and baiting places. Holland. 2. The main point, as of a question; the point on which an action rests; the pith of a matter; as, the gist of a question.
girasol: 1. (Bot.) See Heliotrope. (old) 2. (Min.) A variety of opal which is usually milk white, bluish white, or sky blue; but in a bright light it reflects a reddish color.
gig: A kind of spear or harpoon. See Fishgig. | A playful or wanton girl; a giglot.
gif: If. (old) Note: Gif is the old form of if, and frequently occurs in the earlier English writers. See If.
gin: Against; near by; towards; as, gin night. [Scot.] A. Ross (1778). | To begin; -- often followed by an infinitive without to; as, gan tell. See Gan. [Obs. or Archaic] "He gan to pray." Chaucer.
gibbet: 1. A kind of gallows; an upright post with an arm projecting from the top, on which, formerly, malefactors were hanged in chains, and their bodies allowed to remain asa warning. 2. | 1. To hang and expose on a gibbet. 2. To expose to infamy; to blacken. I'll gibbet up his name. Oldham.
gigget: Same as Gigot. Cut the slaves to giggets. Beau. & Fl.
giglet: A wanton; a lascivious or light, giddy girl. (old) The giglet is willful, and is running upon her fate. Sir W. Scott.
gimlet: A small tool for boring holes. It has a leading screw, a grooved body, and a cross handle. Gimlet eye, a squint-eye. [Colloq.] Wright. | 1. To pierce or make with a gimlet. 2. (Naut.) To turn round (an anchor) by the stock, with a motion like turning a gimlet.
gittern: An instrument like a guitar. "Harps, lutes, and giternes." Chaucer.
gimmal: 1. Joined work whose parts move within each other; a pair or series of interlocked rings. 2. A quaint piece of machinery; a gimmer. (old) | Made or consisting of interlocked rings, gimmal mail. In their pale dull mouths the gimmal bit Lies foul with chewed grass. Shak. Gimmal joint. See Gimbal joint, under Gimbal.
ginger: 1. (Bot.) A plant of the genus Zingiber, of the East and West Indies. The species most known is Z. officinale. 2. The hot and spicy rootstock of Zingiber officinale, which is much used in cookery and in medicine. Ginger beer or ale, a mild beer impregnated with ginger. -- Ginger cordial, a liquor made from ginger, raisins, lemon rind, and water, and sometimes whisky or brandy.
gibbose: Humped; protuberant; -- said of a surface which presents one or more large elevations. Brande & C.
gite: A gown. (old) She came often in a gite of red. Chaucer.
gise: To feed or pasture. (old) | Guise; manner. (old) Chaucer.
giambeux: Greaves; armor for the legs. (old) Spenser.
giusto: In just, correct, or suitable time.
giggot: 1. A leg of mutton. 2. A small piece of flesh; a slice. (old) The rest in giggots cut, they spit. Chapman.
girder: 1. One who, or that which, girds. 2. (Arch. & Engin.) A main beam; a stright, horizontal beam to span an opening or carry weight, such as ends of floor beams, etc.; hence, a framed or built-up member discharging the same office, technically called a compound girder. See Illusts. of Frame, and Doubleframed floor, under Double. Bowstring girder, Box girder, etc.
gibcat: A male cat, esp. an old one. See lst Gib. n. (old) Shak.
giving: 1. The act of bestowing as a gift; a conferring or imparting. 2. A gift; a benefaction. Pope. 3. The act of softening, breaking, or yielding. "Upon the first giving of the weather." Addison. Giving in, a falling inwards; a collapse. -- Giving out, anything uttered or asserted; an outgiving. His givings out were of an infinite distance From his true meant design. Shak.
giereagle: A bird referred to in the Bible (Lev. xi. 18and Deut. xiv. 17) as unclean, probably the Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus).
gillie: A boy or young man; a manservant; a male attendant, in the Scottish Highlands. Sir W. Scott.
girding: That with which one is girded; a girdle. Instead of a stomacher, a girding of sackcloth. Is. iii. 24.
gildale: A drinking bout in which every one pays an equal share. (old)
gird: 1. A stroke with a rod or switch; a severe spasm; a twinge; a pang. Conscience . . . is freed from many fearful girds and twinges which the atheist feels. Tillotson. 2. A cut; a sarcastic remark; | 1. To strike; to smite. (old) To slay him and to girden off his head. Chaucer. 2. To sneer at; to mock; to gibe. Being moved, he will not spare to gird the gods. Shak.
gilder: One who gilds; one whose occupation is to overlay with gold.
